summaries.summary: Spoken Dialogue Systems (SDS) enable natural speech interaction, and task-oriented systems help users achieve goals such as finding restaurants or booking flights.

Task-oriented dialogue management is often formulated as reinforcement learning (RL), where User Simulators train a dialogue manager (DM) policy without real users and enable unlimited faster dialogues.
The Neural User Simulator (NUS) outputs natural language, learns behaviour from a corpus, uses a feature extractor and sequence-to-sequence model, generates goals, and transforms DSTC2 goal-labels.

The NUS is trained on restaurant recommendation dialogues, used to train a reinforcement learning based SDS policy, and outperforms the Agenda-Based User-Simulator (ABUS) in cross-model evaluation and real-user tests.

The paper is organised with Section 2 on task-oriented dialogue, Section 3 on motivation and related work, Section 4 on the NUS, Sections 5 and 6 on experiments and results, and Section 7 on conclusions.
A Task-Oriented SDS uses a structured ontology defining informable slots, requestable slots, restaurants, and slot-value pairs such as area=north.
Using RL, the DM policy maximises cumulative future reward, typically with a small per-turn penalty and a large positive reward for successful interactions.
Training a DM's policy with real users is impractical for most RL algorithms, so learning from a dataset recorded once and reused repeatedly is natural.
Recorded dialogue corpora have limited visited state spaces, often insufficient corpus sizes, and may not contain the optimal dialogue strategy.
A user simulator (US) trained on a dialogue corpus with supervised learning can generate unlimited dialogues and train the DM's policy using feedback from the US or a separate evaluator.

Most user-simulators operate on user semantics, and prior models include bi-gram, graph-based, Markov, hidden Markov, inverse reinforcement learning, Agenda-Based User Simulator, and sequence-to-sequence approaches with various goal limitations.
Semantic-level user simulation raises issues for annotation, joint SLU and belief tracking in DSTC2, and error modelling, motivating natural language user simulators and word-level approaches.

The NUS generates a random goal, uses a Feature Extractor to create feature vectors from SDS output, current goal, and dialogue history, and generates delexicalised utterances while allowing goal changes.
The Goal Generator samples DSTC2 goals with constraints and requests, using probabilities 0.66, 0.62 and 0.58 for food, area and pricerange, and re-samples empty goals.
During sequence-to-sequence training, DSTC2 goal labels are used, but final goals are insufficient for goal changes and turn-specific labels would predict the future.

The proposed update strategy modifies DSTC2 turn-specific constraint labels backwards so goal changes can be replicated during DM policy training, with goals updated when the SDS outputs the canthelp dialogue act.
The Feature Extractor generates feature vectors for the Feature History using DM output, current goal, accepted venue, and current and initial request-vector.
The feature vector consists of four sub-vectors designed to embed the system response while preserving all necessary value-independent information.
The machine-act vector encodes system dialogue acts and slots, with binary representations whose lengths depend on possible system dialogue acts and four times the number of informable slots.
The request-vector tracks unfulfilled requests, is remembered across turns, is reset when a new venue is proposed, and has length equal to the number of requestable slots.
The inconsistency-vector represents misunderstood slots between the system response and the goal, has length equal to the number of informable slots, and lets the NUS correct the system.
The fourth vector is a binary representation of slots in the constraints, has length equal to the number of informable slots, and lets the NUS inform about its preferred venue.
The sequence-to-sequence model consists of an RNN encoder, a fully-connect layer, and an RNN decoder.
At each time-step an RNN uses an input and internal state to produce output and a new state, and this work uses a single layer LSTM with a forget gate without bias and no peep-holes.
The first RNN takes one feature vector at a time, and its final encoder output at the current dialogue turn is passed through a fully-connected layer with linear activation.
For a given encoding, the sequence-to-sequence model defines a probability distribution over sequences, allowing the NUS to generate diverse sentences for the same dialogue context.
The decoder RNN uses 1-hot embeddings of previous words, <SOS> and <EOS> tokens, an affine transform and softmax, and generates words by highest probability or sampling.
During training, true words from the dataset are used instead of sampled words, a technique called teacher-forcing.
Beam-search is deterministic and limits user behaviour diversity, so the NUS uses beam-search with sampling, with 2 beams giving a good trade-off between reasonable responses and diversity.
The neural sequence-to-sequence model is trained to maximize the log probability assigned to user utterances in the training data set.
The network was implemented in Tensorflow, optimized with Adam, used widths of 100, tuned learning rate on validation, used no regularization, and shuffled dialogue turns.

Manual DSTC2 transcriptions were corrected and cleaned, yielding 1609 dialogues with 11638 turns, 505 validation dialogues with 3896 turns, maximum sequence length 22, and maximum dialogue length 30 turns.
Policies were trained in PyDial with NUS or ABUS using GP-SARSA, reward 20 for success and -1 per turn, maximum length 25 turns, metrics SR and average reward, for 4000 dialogues.
The paper argues that fair comparison between a new US model and the ABUS requires indirect evaluation of policies trained with each US.
Cross-model evaluation trains five policies per US with different seeds, reports best and average performance on 1000 test dialogues, and resamples NUS sentences when the new goal is not mentioned.
Human evaluation selected two policies per US, gathered 1000 dialogues with 250 per policy through AMT, used a commercial ASR system, and translated user success judgments into reward.
After 4000 training dialogues, NUS-trained policies achieved average SRs of 94.0% on ABUS and 96.6% on NUS, while ABUS-trained policies achieved 99.5% and 45.5%.
Policies trained on NUS for 1000 dialogues averaged 97.3% SR on ABUS versus 94.0% after 4000 dialogues, indicating overfitting to the NUS across all five seeds.
In human evaluation over 250 dialogues per policy, the best NUS-trained policy achieved 93.4% success rate and 13.8 average rewards, versus 90.0% and 13.3 for ABUS.
The Neural User Simulator uses semantic system responses as input, produces natural language responses, requires less labelling, and excelled in simulated-user and real-user policy evaluations.
The research was partly funded by EPSRC grant EP/M018946/1 Open Domain Statistical Spoken Dialogue Systems, with support for Florian Kreyssig and Paweł Budzianowski from named organizations.
